header: (Dr. Omar Chughtai and 02 others Vs. Province of Punjab & 02
J U D G M E N T
body: Date of hearing. 20.10.2026.
Appellants by:- M/s. Muhammad Shan Gull & Obaid Ullah, Advocates.
Respondents by:- Mr. Zafar Iqbal Sheikh, Advocate.
Province of Punjab by:- Rai Mazhar Hussain Kharal, Assistant Advocate General, Punjab.

TANVEER AHMAD SHEIKH, J.:- This Intra Court Appeal has been directed against the order dated 16.05.2024, passed by learned single Judge in Chamber in Writ Petition No. 2863 of 2024, whereby petition was dismissed and order dated 27.03.2024 passed by, respondent No.2/District and Sessions Judge/Presiding Officer, District Consumer Court, Bahawalnagar (hereinafter called as consumer court) dismissing the application seeking the rejection/return of complaint was maintained. .

2. According to the brief facts gleaned out of present appeal are that respondent No.3 (Tabassum Ijaz) hired the services of appellant/clinical lab for carrying out certain clinical tests and the result of tests was found to be inaccurate, which constrained him to file a complaint before respondent No.2/learned consumer court, with the averments that on 30.08.2023, he deposited his blood samples for his tests Plasma Glucose (Fasting), Plasma Glucose (2 hrs and Postprandial) Glycosylated Hemoglobin (HBa 1C) and Serum Total Cholesterol. He received test reports from the collection center of appellants lab collection center at Haroonabad on 04.09.2023, which were inaccurate, fake, false and fictitious, therefore, he lodged his protest to appellant No.3 (Chughtai Lab Collection Centre, Haroonabad), who again got sent blood samples of respondent No.3 (Tabassum Ijaz) to another lab and as per report of other lab, the result of appellant lab (Chughtai Lab) was found to be inaccurate. Respondent No.3 got issued a notice to appellant lab in terms of Section 28 and ultimately filed a complaint under Section 25 of Punjab Consumer Protection Act, 2005 (herein after as called Act, 2005).
3. Learned counsel for appellants/lab presented written arguments, wherein he mainly focused on the points that according to section 2(k) of PCP Act 2005 the term “services” shall not cover therein .

“diagnostic services”; the matter is amenable to the jurisdiction of Punjab Healthcare Commission (Commission) constituted under the Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010, who was empowered to deal with the complaints regarding the provisions of defective medical and medical diagnostic services; added that the definition of “Healthcare Establishment” shall also include “Diagnostic Centre” (Section 2(xv) and 2(xvi) of PHC Act, 2010; next added that since subject matter of “diagnostic services” is specifically mentioned in PHC Act, 2010, as such even if the inclusive definition of “services” provided in PCP Act, 2005 is adopted to confer jurisdiction to consumer court, even then existence of more special law (PHC Act, 2010) caring non obstentee clause (Section 28) dealing specifically with medical and diagnostic services, shall prevail over special law i.e. PCP Act, 2005, which was kept in addition to and not in derogation of the other laws (Section 3); also added that an aggrieved person may have a resort to law of tort for the recovery damages after the matter has been adjudicated upon by a Commission and the service provider has been declared as negligent.
4. Conversely, the learned counsel for respondent No.3 (Tabassum Ijaz) supported the impugned order and alleged that PHC Act, 2010 provides mechanism for the imposition of .

fine/penalty upon the service provider, but not for compensation for an aggrieved person, as such orders passed by learned consumer court as well as learned single Judge in Chamber are not open to any exception.
5. Arguments heard. File perused.

6. Said controversy /proposition of law requires thorough, complete and detailed study, and critical analysis of provisions of Section 4,19,22,23,28,29 and 30 of Punjab Healthcare Commission Act 2010 and provisions of Section 2 (k), 3,13,25,31 and 37 of Punjab Consumer Protection Act 2005, which are being produced below for the facility of reference The Punjab Healthcare Commission Act 2010 (hereinafter called Act 2010)

Punjab Consumer protection act 2005 (hereinafter called as Ac of 2005)
Sec: 2(k) – “services” includes the provision of any kind of facilities or advice or assistance such as provision of medical, legal or engineering services.
Sec: 3. Act not in derogation of any other law.- the provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in Derogation of the Provisions of any other Law for the time being in force.
Sec: 13. Liability for faulty or defective services. A provider of such services shall be liable to a consumer for damages proximately caused by the provision of services that have caused damage.
Sec: 25. Filing of claims. A claim for damages arising out of contravention of any provisions of this Act shall be filed before a Consumer Court set up under this Act.

Sec: 31. Order of consumer court. If after the proceedings conducted under this Act, the Consumer Court is satisfied that the products complained against suffer from any of the defects specified in the claim or that any or all of the allegations contained in the claim about the services provided are true, it shall issue an order to the defendant directing him to take one or more of the following actions, namely:- (a) to remove defect from the products in question, (b) to replace the products with new products of similar description which shall be free from any defect, (c) to return to the claimant the price or, as the case may be, the charges paid by the claimant, (d) to do such other things as may be necessary for adequate and proper compliance with the requirements of this Act, .

(e) to pay reasonable compensation to the consumer for any loss suffered by him due to the negligence of the defendant, (f) to award damages where appropriate, (g) to award actual costs including lawyer’s fees incurred on the legal proceedings, (h) to recall the product from trade or commerce, (i) to confiscate or destroy the defective product, (j) to remedy the defect in such period as may be deemed fit, or (k) to cease to provide the defective or faulty service until it achieves the required standard.

7. So far as PHC Act 2010 is concerned, according to its preamble, it was enacted for the establishment of Punjab Healthcare Commission, to make provisions for the improvement of quality of healthcare services, to ban quackery in all its forms and manifestations and to provide for ancillary matters. Section 4 (2)(e) thereof dealing with the powers and functions of the commission empowers the commission to inquire into and investigate the matters of malpractices and failures in the provision of healthcare services. Clause (g) further authorizes the commission to impose fine and collect penalties on violations, breach, or non compliance of the provisions, rules, standing orders and instructions. Under clause (q) commission may also take necessary steps to ban quackery. Section 4 (7) of Act 2010 is a “non obstente clause”, which commences from the words “notwithstanding anything contained in any .

other law” and authorizes the commission to undertake investigation into allegations of maladministration, malpractice or failure on the part of healthcare service provider, or any employee of the healthcare service provider.

Under Section 18 of Act 2010 Commission may revoke or suspend the license of a healthcare service provider, if obtained through fraud or misrepresentation and under section 19 commission may declare a healthcare service provider to be guilty for medical negligence due to the none availability of requisite man resources or equipment’s, or failure in exercising with reasonable competence the skill, which service provider or its employee possess. Section 22 (2) and (4) of Act 2010 empowers the inspection team formed by commission to inspect any healthcare establishment on receipt of complaint and to inquire into on the allegation of maladministration, malpractice or failure in the provisions of healthcare services. Subsection 5 thereof further authorizes the commission to impose a fine upon healthcare service provider which may extend to fifty thousand rupees.

Section 23 (2) of Act of 2010 envisages that any aggrieved person may file a compliant before the commission against a healthcare service provider within 60 days from the date of knowledge of cause of action.

Under Section 28 of act of 2010 commission has a power to impose a fine up to five lac rupees on the complaint of any aggrieved person after providing right of audience to the parties having regard to the gravity of offence.

Section 29 of the Act has ousted the jurisdiction of other forums and claimed that no suit, prosecution and other legal proceedings relating to healthcare services shall lie against a healthcare service provider except under this Act. Moreover, under section 30 of Act of 2010 District & Sessions Judge has been empowered to question the validity of actions taken or intended to be taken, or orders made and intended to be made, or to grant interim injunctions as an Appellant Authority/Court constituted under Section 31 thereof.

8. On the other hand Act of 2005 was promulgated for the protection and promotion of the rights and interests of consumers, speedy redressal of consumer complaints and for matters connected herewith, (preamble)
9. PCP Act 2005 does not contain any “non obstante clause” to give it an overriding effect and the Act was kept in addition to and not in derogation of the other laws (Section 3).

Section 2 of the Act 2005 is definition clause and clause (k) thereof has widened the scope of term “services” and, in addition to its ordinary meaning, also included therein all kinds of facilities, or advice, or assistance such as provision of medical, legal or engineering services. Medical service was mentioned therein in specific and clear terms, which leaves no room for any ambiguity.

Section 13 of Act of 2005 makes a service provider liable for damages proximately cause by provision of faulty/defective services. Under section 25 of the Act an aggrieved person may file a claim before a consumer court for .
damages arising out of contravention of any of the provisions of the Act.
Section 31 the Act prescribes all kinds of the orders, reliefs and compensations, which a consumer court may pass, grant and award after adjudication of a matter.

10. When provisions of both the enactments are read in its contexts and kept into juxtaposition to each other, it emerges after careful examination that both the enactments deal with the complaints against healthcare service provider for maladministration, malpractices, unreasonable and unskillful treatment and provide independent forums under the respective provisions thereof. So much so Act 2010 also contains “non obstente clause” (Sec: 28-29) regarding its applicability ousting the jurisdiction and operation of other laws, but proceedings/ prosecution initiated, or an action taken under the PHC Act 2010 shall culminate into the revocation/suspension of license of healthcare service provider, or imposition of fine/penalty etc. It does not provide any system /mechanism/scheme for the award of compensation and damages to an aggrieved person, which is exclusively and purely subject matter of PCP Act 2005 and within the domain of Consumer Court. An aggrieved person may have a resort to consumer court for the recovery of compensation/damages for malpractices/maladministration and provision of unreasonable and unskillful treatment. In a claim .

instituted under the act of 2005, consumer court may pass an order for the payment of reasonable compensation to the consumer for any loss suffered by him, award of damages, award of actual costs including lawyer’s fees incurred on the legal proceedings (section 32). A consumer court has no power to revoke, or suspend the license of healthcare service provider or to impose penalties on certain violations.

11. Combined effect of above discussion and critical analysis of relevant provisions of both the enactment is that subject matter of both the enactments is separate and independent, which do not overlap each other, therefore carrying a “none obstantee clause” by Act of 2010 (Section 29) is of no significance. There is no need to invoke the doctrine of implied repeal for help. We feel no hesitation in holding that complaint before consumer court against healthcare service provider for the recovery of compensation /damages etc. is maintainable. Even remedy under both the enactments can be availed simultaneously and section 4 (11) of Act 2010, which restrains the commission from taking the cognizance of a matter sub-judice before a competent court, shall not operate as a bar, which reads as under, SEC: 4 (11). The Commission shall not investigate or inquire into any matter subjudice before a Court of competent jurisdiction on the date of the receipt of a complaint, reference or motion.

12. Next objection raised by learned counsel for appellant was that no claim for the compensation or damages can be filed before the consumer Court unless allegation of maladministration or malpractice is adjudicated upon first by the commission. Said contention is not tenable. It does not appear to be the intent of enactment. The learned Single Judge in Chamber answered the said objection in the following terms:- “Argument that no claim of damages could be filed unless allegation of maladministration or malpractice is adjudicated upon and endorsed by the Commission is misconceived. Role of the Commission to act as gatekeeper for determining the existence and pursuit of damages is mere figment of imagination, and not conceived by the provisions of Act 2010. Learned counsel for the petitioner failed to give any explanation when confronted with the mandate of sub-section (11) of section 4 of Act, 2010 (supra).”

Conclusion arrived at by learned Single Judge in this regard is based upon correct interpretation of law. Therefore, we also reject the said contention outrightly, because there is a clear distinction in the scope of jurisdiction exercised by commission and available to consumer Court.

13. The term ‘Services’ used in Section 2(k) of PCP Act, 2005 shall be given broader, extensive and comprehensive meaning. The word ‘service’ is a versatile English word that generally means doing work, help, or an action that benefits someone else. .

Diagnostic procedures are always considered as integral part of medical & health care services, as such it shall also include therein “medical diagnostic services”. Diagnostic tests are always regarded as core component of a patient evaluation, disease detection and treatment planning. Therefore, diagnostic error, mis-diagnosis, use of substandard equipments, delayed result of test, over charging by a diagnostic lab/hospital can be challenged as deficiency in the service before district consumer court.

14. Claim of the learned counsel that the definition of ‘Healthcare Establishment’ provided in Section 2(xv) of PHC Act, 2010 includes ‘diagnostic center’, therein specifically when read with the jurisdiction ouster clause (Section 28) shall confer the jurisdiction to commission excluding the Consumer Court to entertain the complaints regarding the provision of faulty diagnostic services is misconceived, because subject matter of both the above enactments is different as discussed above. Remedy before the commission seeking the imposition of penalty upon medical diagnostic service/lab service provider can also be availed separately and independently, which does not dislodge the jurisdiction of Consumer Court being on different subject matter.
15. It is also noteworthy that although PCP Act, 2005 is a special law, but it has been kept in addition .

to and not in derogation of other laws for the time being in force (Section 3). It does not contain any nonobstante clause to give it an overriding effect. It means that it supplements other existing laws rather replacing and overriding them, unless a direct conflict, or an explicit overriding clause, or a specialized legislative intend dictates otherwise. Both the enactments can operate side by side without adversely affecting each other.

16. When an aggrieved person has multiple or concurrent legal forums for a cause of action, he may choose any one of those parallel forums. Thereafter, he is bound by his choice. After election of the forum or remedy, he cannot thereafter abandon an already chosen forum/remedy halfway to “hop over and shop” for another parallel remedy. He cannot switch from one forum to another forum. By applying the principal of election, he cannot be permitted from invoking the other parallel jurisdiction, because he is prevented from having another bite of the cherry.

17. Therefore, we are of the confirmed view that if an aggrieved person files his lis before the court of ordinary jurisdiction (Civil Court) under the law of tort for the recovery of damages on account of provision of defective product or faulty service, the proceedings before the civil court cannot be termed as coram non judice, but thereafter he cannot have resort to another .
forum. Contention of learned counsel for appellant that grievance agitated by respondent No.3, is exclusively amendable to the jurisdiction of Civil Court, is not acceptable in the eye of law.

18. We found that impugned order passed by learned Single Judge in Chamber is well reasoned and within the four corners of law. Learned counsel for appellant when asked, failed to point out any illegality, or material irregularity, or jurisdictional error in the same, he miserably failed to do so. Impugned order does not call for any interference. Present appeal has no force, we dismissed the same accordingly. (Ch. Sultan Mahmood) (Tanveer Ahmad Sheikh) Judge Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING.
Judge Judge *Shahzad Ahmad Nasir*
